metadata.title: Partners Joining or Leaving at Different Times
metadata.description: Build each partner’s active investment period from a shared business timeline.
metadata.teachingApproach: Develop the capital-time model step by step; use timelines and segment ledgers; show intermediate calculations, unit and share checks, and topic-specific remedial feedback. Practice uses fresh values aligned to the approved scope.
metadata.sourceScope: R. S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude, Chapter 14: Partnership (printed pp. 476–492). Approved scope: Draw a business timeline, identify the total partnership term, and convert entry or exit dates into each partner’s duration. Use the remaining months (not elapsed months) for a late entrant, and split a year correctly when a partner exits early. Combine each duration with its capital and compare capital-time products. Include two- and three-partner timelines, month/year changes, and a check that durations fit within the stated term. Ground in solved examples 2, 9–11 and objective patterns 10, 12–20, 47–50, and 57–60.

content.text: Partners Joining or Leaving at Different Times: Build each partner’s active investment period from a shared business timeline. This lesson builds a partnership model, explains each step, works through examples, and offers fresh practice with targeted recovery.

Partners Joining or Leaving at Different Times asks you to decide what determines each partner’s share. Build each partner’s active investment period from a shared business timeline. We will build the model from the agreement, calculate a representative case, and test the result against the original conditions.

Start with the quantity the agreement actually rewards. In ordinary partnership profit sharing, that is the capital made available to the business over time. A timeline turns phrases such as “joined after five months” into a precise investment duration. Write the partner names and the stated basis before you choose an operation.

The core model is: each partner’s weight = capital × time invested. This follows by comparing equal units of capital-month: twice the capital for the same duration contributes twice as much, and the same capital held twice as long also contributes twice as much.

For a T-month business, joining after x months means investing for T−x months; leaving after x months means investing for x months. Keep the capital amount and its time period in separate columns first. Only multiply once both are expressed in compatible units; this makes the origin of every ratio term visible.

Worked reasoning: In a 12-month business, A invests all year and B joins after month 4. Their durations are 12 and 8 months, not 4 and 12. Notice that the ratio comes from relative contribution, not from the order in which partners are named or from who manages the business. Preserve the labels until the final allocation.

When the total profit is known, add the reduced ratio terms to find total parts. Divide the distributable profit by those parts for one part, then multiply by the requested partner’s parts. Do not treat a ratio term itself as a rupee amount.

Use the timeline or agreement to identify intervals before doing arithmetic. Label whether x means elapsed time or time invested every time it appears. If a partner’s capital changes, record the new amount only from the date it takes effect; if a time factor is common to everyone, cancel it only after forming the ratio.

A second way to check the model is to rebuild each partner’s contribution independently. Draw month 0 and month T, then mark every entry and exit. Confirm all durations lie between 0 and T. If the resulting ratio reverses a known relationship—for example, a larger weighted contribution receiving a smaller share—inspect the partner labels and ratio order.

Watch for this error: The entry delay and the duration are complementary quantities; confusing them reverses the profit ratio. Another frequent slip is to use elapsed time instead of invested time. Mark the start and end of each interval; for a late entrant in a T-month business, invested duration is T minus the delay.

A useful worked check is to allocate the full pool and add the receipts. For partner i, the share is total profit × (i’s weight / all partners’ weights). This fraction must be between 0 and 1 for positive weights, and all partner fractions must sum to 1.

Translate special wording before calculation. A percentage increase may refer to original capital, a withdrawal may be partial, and an allowance may be removed before investment-based sharing. For equal profit shares, the two capital-time products must be equal; this gives an equation for an unknown joining date. Underline the base of each percentage and state whether the pool is original or remaining profit.

If an unknown amount or date is requested, set up the relationship before solving. Equate the capital-time products in the stated profit ratio, or write a share as its fraction of total profit. Keep unknowns tied to their partner labels and check that a date remains within the business term.

If your first answer seems wrong, revisit the model rather than repeating the arithmetic. Ask: did I use the right basis, include every interval, convert all time units, and use the right total pool? Then substitute the candidate into the original data and recompute the ratio.

For a timed exam, use a compact ledger: partner; capital in each interval; months in that interval; weighted contribution; share fraction. Reduce large products by common factors only after they are formed, and keep exact fractions until the final currency amount.

Mastery check: explain why the chosen weights represent the agreement, show one intermediate calculation, and verify the final share or sufficiency conclusion. You should now be able to solve the approved scope for partners joining or leaving at different times without relying on a memorized answer pattern.

A invests ₹76000 for a 12-month business. B invests ₹57000 and joins later. If A:B profit shares are 2:1, how many months after the start did B join?

inlineData.prompt: A invests ₹76000 for a 12-month business. B invests ₹57000 and joins later. If A:B profit shares are 2:1, how many months after the start did B join?
hints: Distinguish B’s months invested from the delay before B joined.
First solve B's duration from C_A T : C_B t = 2:1; subtract that duration from 12.
inlineData.explanation: A's capital-time is 76000×12=912000. For ratio 2:1, B's required weight is 456000; at ₹57000 per month B's duration is 8 months. Thus B joined after 12−8=4 months. Verify by substituting both weights.
